sections.purpose: To correctly use a stethoscope for auscultation of heart sounds, lung sounds, and bowel sounds as part of clinical pharmacology and pharmacy practice training.
sections.scope: Applicable to Pharmacology laboratory for clinical skills development, including cardiac and pulmonary auscultation practicals.
procedure: Insert the earpieces of the stethoscope into the ear canals with the tips angled slightly forward to seal the ear canal.
Tap the diaphragm gently to confirm you can hear the sound through the earpieces.

Select the appropriate chest piece side: Diaphragm (flat side, firm pressure) for high-frequency sounds (normal heart/lung sounds, bowel sounds); Bell (cup side, light pressure) for low-frequency sounds (S3, S4 gallops, mitral stenosis murmurs).
Ask the subject to sit or lie comfortably and expose the area to be auscultated.
Place the chest piece directly on the skin — do not auscultate over clothing.
For heart sounds: Auscultate at the 4 standard positions — Aortic (2nd right ICS), Pulmonic (2nd left ICS), Tricuspid (4th left ICS), Mitral/Apex (5th left ICS, mid-clavicular line).
Listen for S1 (lub) and S2 (dub) sounds at each position; note any abnormal sounds (murmurs, clicks, rubs).
For lung sounds: Ask the subject to breathe deeply and slowly through the mouth while auscultating all lung fields bilaterally.
Listen for normal breath sounds (vesicular, bronchial, bronchovesicular) and note any adventitious sounds (crackles, wheezes, rhonchi).
Record all auscultatory findings systematically with the position and nature of sounds heard.
Clean the earpieces and chest piece with a 70% alcohol swab after each use.
Store the stethoscope in its designated case or hanging rack — avoid coiling tightly around the neck for storage.
precautions: Always warm the chest piece with your hands before placing on a subject's skin.
Maintain complete silence during auscultation — ambient noise significantly affects sound quality.
Use appropriate pressure: firm pressure for diaphragm, light pressure for bell — pressing the bell too hard converts it to a diaphragm.
Never auscultate over clothing, hair, or wound dressings — place directly on skin.
Clean the stethoscope between subjects to prevent cross-contamination — use 70% isopropyl alcohol.
Inspect tubing for cracks or holes regularly — damaged tubing reduces sound transmission.
Check earpiece fit and angle — improperly fitted earpieces significantly reduce sound quality.
Do not expose the stethoscope to extreme heat, organic solvents, or oils.
